report:
**Yes, the evidence supports that widespread mask-wearing reduces COVID-19 infections at the population level.**

Here is a summary of the key evidence:

1. **A large randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Bangladesh** (the only major community-level RCT on masking) found that promoting mask-wearing reduced symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections by roughly 9–11% overall, with a 35% reduction among people aged 60 and older. Surgical masks were particularly effective. ([The Conversation](https://theconversation.com/evidence-shows-that-yes-masks-prevent-covid-19-and-surgical-masks-are-the-way-to-go-167963))

2. **A PNAS study directly measuring population mask-wearing** (not just mandates) found that mean mask-wearing levels corresponded to a 19% decrease in SARS-CoV-2 transmission, concluding that "population mask wearing notably reduced SARS-CoV-2 transmission." ([PNAS, 2022](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2119266119))

3. **A WHO-sponsored systematic review** (Chu et al.) found that "face mask use could result in a large reduction in risk of infection," alongside physical distancing and eye protection. ([PNAS evidence review](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2014564118))

4. **A 2025 systematic literature review** published in MDPI concluded that "masking policies and mask wearing are beneficial to prevent and reduce the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infections and COVID-19 disease in various real-world settings." ([MDPI, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/22/10/1590))

5. **U.S. state-level observational research** found that states with higher mask adherence had lower COVID-19 case growth rates. ([PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0249891))

**Conclusion:** Multiple lines of evidence — including an RCT, observational studies, and systematic reviews — converge on the finding that when a large proportion of the population wears masks, COVID-19 transmission and infection rates decline. The effect is strongest for older individuals and when surgical masks are used. While the magnitude of reduction varies by study and setting, the overall body of evidence supports your answer of "yes."
